questions.q: In the case study, why is inventory count treated as eventually consistent (AP) rather than strongly consistent?
options: Because inventory data is never important to the business
Because a few seconds of staleness is an acceptable trade-off, and refusing to show the page at all to guarantee perfect freshness would hurt the business more
Because strongly consistent data cannot be stored in any database
Because the CAP theorem forbids inventory systems from choosing consistency
questions.explain: The case study deliberately favors availability for inventory count: showing slightly stale stock is less costly to the business than refusing to serve the page, and an occasional oversell can be resolved afterward.

questions.q: Why does the case study treat payment state differently from inventory, choosing strong consistency (CP)?
options: Because payment data is stored on a different continent
Because the system would rather briefly refuse to confirm a charge than risk two conflicting records of whether a customer was charged
Because payment processors never experience network partitions
Because CP and AP are interchangeable terms with no real difference
questions.explain: For payment state, correctness matters more than always answering immediately, so the system favors consistency — refusing to confirm rather than risk an incorrect or duplicated charge record.

questions.q: Why does checkout publish an "order placed" message to a queue instead of calling the fulfillment system directly?
options: So that checkout can succeed and return to the customer immediately even if fulfillment is temporarily unavailable, with the message waiting in the queue until fulfillment is ready
Because direct calls between services are technically impossible
Because queues guarantee strong consistency automatically
Because fulfillment never needs to process the order at all
questions.explain: Using a queue decouples checkout from fulfillment's availability — the customer's checkout doesn't fail just because fulfillment happens to be down at that moment; the message simply waits.

questions.q: Why is an idempotency key attached to the retried payment charge request?
options: To make the charge process faster
So that if the original attempt actually succeeded and only its response was lost, the retry safely returns the original result instead of charging the customer a second time
To permanently disable retries
Because idempotency keys are required by every network protocol
questions.explain: The timeout on the payment call means the checkout service can't tell if the first charge succeeded or not. An idempotency key lets a retry safely deduplicate against a charge that may have already gone through.

questions.q: What is the main lesson of reading a system design the way this case study does?
options: Every system must make the exact same CAP trade-off for all of its data
Different pieces of the same system can reasonably make different consistency/availability trade-offs, and recognizing where and why is the actual skill
Message queues should never be used in checkout systems
Idempotency keys are only relevant to Salesforce governor limits
questions.explain: The case study shows that a single system applies multiple distinct patterns and trade-offs (per-data CAP choices, queue decoupling, idempotent retries) rather than one blanket decision, and identifying those choices is the durable skill being taught.
